lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: CHAPTER II. The Pool of Tears

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Curiouser and curiouser!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English);

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “now I’m opening out like the largest telescope that ever was! Good-bye, feet!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: (for when she looked down at her feet, they seemed to be almost out of sight, they were getting so far off).

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh, my poor little feet, I wonder who will put on your shoes and stockings for you now, dears? I’m sure I shan’t be able! I shall be a great deal too far off to trouble myself about you: you must manage the best way you can;—but I must be kind to them,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought Alice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “or perhaps they won’t walk the way I want to go! Let me see: I’ll give them a new pair of boots every Christmas.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And she went on planning to herself how she would manage it.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “They must go by the carrier,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she thought;

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “and how funny it’ll seem, sending presents to one’s own feet! And how odd the directions will look!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text:
Alice’s Right Foot, Esq.,
Hearthrug,
near the Fender,
(with Alice’s love).

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Oh dear, what nonsense I’m talking!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Just then her head struck against the roof of the hall: in fact she was now more than nine feet high, and she at once took up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Poor Alice! It was as much as she could do, lying down on one side, to look through into the garden with one eye; but to get through was more hopeless than ever: she sat down and began to cry again.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “You ought to be ashamed of yourself,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “a great girl like you,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: (she might well say this),

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “to go on crying in this way! Stop this moment, I tell you!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: But she went on all the same, shedding gallons of tears, until there was a large pool all round her, about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: After a time she heard a little pattering of feet in the distance, and she hastily dried her eyes to see what was coming. It was the White Rabbit returning, splendidly dressed, with a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other: he came trotting along in a great hurry, muttering to himself as he came,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice felt so desperate that she was ready to ask help of any one; so, when the Rabbit came near her, she began, in a low, timid voice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “If you please, sir—”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Rabbit started violently, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and skurried away into the darkness as hard as he could go.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice took up the fan and gloves, and, as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself all the time she went on talking:

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Dear, dear! How queer everything is to-day! And yesterday things went on just as usual. I wonder if I’ve been changed in the night? Let me think: was I the same when I got up this morning? I almost think I can remember feeling a little different. But if I’m not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: And she began thinking over all the children she knew that were of the same age as herself, to see if she could have been changed for any of them.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’m sure I’m not Ada,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “for her hair goes in such long ringlets, and mine doesn’t go in ringlets at all; and I’m sure I can’t be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things, and she, oh! she knows such a very little! Besides, she’s she, and I’m I, and—oh dear, how puzzling it all is! I’ll try if I know all the things I used to know. Let me see: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen, and four times seven is—oh dear! I shall never get to twenty at that rate! However, the Multiplication Table doesn’t signify: let’s try Geography. London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome, and Rome—no, that’s all wrong, I’m certain! I must have been changed for Mabel! I’ll try and say ‘How doth the little—’”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: and she crossed her hands on her lap as if she were saying lessons, and began to repeat it, but her voice sounded hoarse and strange, and the words did not come the same as they used to do:—

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text:
“How doth the little crocodile
Improve his shining tail,
And pour the waters of the Nile
On every golden scale!
“How cheerfully he seems to grin,
How neatly spread his claws,
And welcome little fishes in
With gently smiling jaws!”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’m sure those are not the right words,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said poor Alice, and her eyes filled with tears again as she went on,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I must be Mabel after all, and I shall have to go and live in that poky little house, and have next to no toys to play with, and oh! ever so many lessons to learn! No, I’ve made up my mind about it; if I’m Mabel, I’ll stay down here! It’ll be no use their putting their heads down and saying ‘Come up again, dear!’ I shall only look up and say ‘Who am I then? Tell me that first, and then, if I like being that person, I’ll come up: if not, I’ll stay down here till I’m somebody else’—but, oh dear!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice, with a sudden burst of tears,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I do wish they would put their heads down! I am so very tired of being all alone here!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: As she said this she looked down at her hands, and was surprised to see that she had put on one of the Rabbit’s little white kid gloves while she was talking.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “How can I have done that?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she thought.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “I must be growing small again.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: She got up and went to the table to measure herself by it, and found that, as nearly as she could guess, she was now about two feet high, and was going on shrinking rapidly: she soon found out that the cause of this was the fan she was holding, and she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “That was a narrow escape!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, a good deal frightened at the sudden change, but very glad to find herself still in existence;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and now for the garden!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: and she ran with all speed back to the little door: but, alas! the little door was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table as before,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and things are worse than ever,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought the poor child,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “for I never was so small as this before, never! And I declare it’s too bad, that it is!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: As she said these words her foot slipped, and in another moment, splash! she was up to her chin in salt water. Her first idea was that she had somehow fallen into the sea,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and in that case I can go back by railway,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: she said to herself. (Alice had been to the seaside once in her life, and had come to the general conclusion, that wherever you go to on the English coast you find a number of bathing machines in the sea, some children digging in the sand with wooden spades, then a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station.) However, she soon made out that she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I wish I hadn’t cried so much!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, as she swam about, trying to find her way out.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I shall be punished for it now, I suppose, by being drowned in my own tears! That will be a queer thing, to be sure! However, everything is queer to-day.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Just then she heard something splashing about in the pool a little way off, and she swam nearer to make out what it was: at first she thought it must be a walrus or hippopotamus, but then she remembered how small she was now, and she soon made out that it was only a mouse that had slipped in like herself.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Would it be of any use, now,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought Alice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “to speak to this mouse? Everything is so out-of-the-way down here, that I should think very likely it can talk: at any rate, there’s no harm in trying.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So she began:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “O Mouse, do you know the way out of this pool? I am very tired of swimming about here, O Mouse!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: (Alice thought this must be the right way of speaking to a mouse: she had never done such a thing before, but she remembered having seen in her brother’s Latin Grammar,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: ) The Mouse looked at her rather inquisitively, and seemed to her to wink with one of its little eyes, but it said nothing.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Perhaps it doesn’t understand English,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: thought Alice;

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I daresay it’s a French mouse, come over with William the Conqueror.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: (For, with all her knowledge of history, Alice had no very clear notion how long ago anything had happened.) So she began again:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Où est ma chatte?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: which was the first sentence in her French lesson-book. The Mouse gave a sudden leap out of the water, and seemed to quiver all over with fright.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Oh, I beg your pardon!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice hastily, afraid that she had hurt the poor animal’s feelings.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I quite forgot you didn’t like cats.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Not like cats!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried the Mouse, in a shrill, passionate voice.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “Would you like cats if you were me?”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Well, perhaps not,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice in a soothing tone:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “don’t be angry about it. And yet I wish I could show you our cat Dinah: I think you’d take a fancy to cats if you could only see her. She is such a dear quiet thing,”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: Alice went on, half to herself, as she swam lazily about in the pool,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “and she sits purring so nicely by the fire, licking her paws and washing her face—and she is such a nice soft thing to nurse—and she’s such a capital one for catching mice—oh, I beg your pardon!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice again, for this time the Mouse was bristling all over, and she felt certain it must be really offended.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “We won’t talk about her any more if you’d rather not.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “We indeed!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried the Mouse, who was trembling down to the end of his tail.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: “As if I would talk on such a subject! Our family always hated cats: nasty, low, vulgar things! Don’t let me hear the name again!”

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I won’t indeed!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: said Alice, in a great hurry to change the subject of conversation.

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Are you—are you fond—of—of dogs?”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: The Mouse did not answer, so Alice went on eagerly:

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “There is such a nice little dog near our house I should like to show you! A little bright-eyed terrier, you know, with oh, such long curly brown hair! And it’ll fetch things when you throw them, and it’ll sit up and beg for its dinner, and all sorts of things—I can’t remember half of them—and it belongs to a farmer, you know, and he says it’s so useful, it’s worth a hundred pounds! He says it kills all the rats and—oh dear!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: cried Alice in a sorrowful tone,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “I’m afraid I’ve offended it again!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: For the Mouse was swimming away from her as hard as it could go, and making quite a commotion in the pool as it went.

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: So she called softly after it,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Mouse dear! Do come back again, and we won’t talk about cats or dogs either, if you don’t like them!”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: When the Mouse heard this, it turned round and swam slowly back to her: its face was quite pale (with passion, Alice thought), and it said in a low trembling voice,

lines.speaker: Alice
lines.text: “Let us get to the shore, and then I’ll tell you my history, and you’ll understand why it is I hate cats and dogs.”

lines.speaker: Narrator
lines.text: It was high time to go, for the pool was getting quite crowded with the birds and animals that had fallen into it: there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet, and several other curious creatures. Alice led the way, and the whole party swam to the shore.
